items.title: The Logistics of NYC Waste Management
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
New York City has 8.5 million people living within the city limits, which are in a relatively small area compared to other large cities. Manhattan has more than 70,000 people per square mile, stacked atop each other in tall buildings, all producing garbage everyday. Where does all that garbage go? Up until 2001, it was taken to a landfill on Staten Island, but Fresh Kills was never adequate or safe. And you can't just dump all that trash in the ocean.

New York City employees more than 9,000 people to deal with garbage, and there are thousands more working for private companies under city contracts. They collect trash every day, compact it, load it onto huge containers, and send it by train to far-flung parts of the country. Half as Interesting explains the complex logistics of dealing with trash in a system most New Yorkers know little about, and don't want to think about. The video is only 5:45, the rest is an ad.

items.title: A 5-Year-Old's Questions for Google Home
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
A father who is totally embracing modern technology discovers that Google Home had saved a year's worth of data, including his 5-year-old son's questions. He is charmed by his son's curiosity about the world, and appreciates the funny parts.

Rowan's questions are adorable.  On the other hand, it's a bit creepy to think that all these commands to an app are recorded for someone else to find, and for Google to analyze and market.

My children came to me with incessant questions about the world throughout their childhoods, which I tried my best to answer, even if I had to look it up. As a result, they thought I was the repository of all the world's wisdom. They know better now, but I wouldn't trade that experience for all the chocolate. (via

Laughing Squid)

items.title: The Biggest Ball of Twine
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
In 1989, Weird Al Yankovic included a song called

"The Biggest Ball of Twine in Minnesota" on his album UHF – Original Motion Picture Soundtrack and Other Stuff. The song was not in the movie, and was never released as a single. But it referenced a real story. 

In 1950, Francis A. Johnson of Darwin, Minnesota, started collecting sisal twine from hay baling. He rolled it into a ball that became enormous, and made the papers. But then Frank Stoeber of Cawker City, Kansas, decided to give Johnson a run for his money, and the race to get into the Guinness Book of World Records was on. You might even call it a war. 

Drunk History gave Patton Oswalt all the Scotch whisky he could drink and had him tell the story of the world's biggest ball of twine. It features special appearances by Colin Hanks, Seth Green, Steve Agee, and Weird Al Yankovic. Oswalt kept up pretty well considering, until he was asked to give us the moral of the story. At least he tried. This video contains NSFW language.

items.title: Which is Better: Buying or Renting a Home?
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content: Is it better to rent a home or buy one? It all depends. The TED-Ed lesson compares two people who made different choices. The amounts of money thrown around here are scary, because I've never had that much. But it's all relative. I told my kids to buy a house once they've decided where they want to live for many years to come. Otherwise, rent until you are ready to settle down. Princess bought one, where her kids can make all the noise they want. Dr. Dolittle rents. She and her husband come to my house and cosplay as house owners, mowing my lawn and doing other maintenance. Personally, I get a lot of satisfaction out of owning my home, but I never had to sign a 30-year mortgage. That's really scary.

items.title: The Real Meaning of Real Extreme Temperatures
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
How hot can it get? How cold can it get? Here on earth, temperatures fluctuate wildly, but they mostly stay in the sweet spot where we can survive (Antarctica and Death Valley excluded). but in the science of measuring temperature, physicists look at the activity of atoms. There is a temperature called absolute zero, but we've never seen it and can't achieve it. We came close once, and some really weird things happened. When we take the temperature up, exploding stars are the hottest things we can think of. How can we measure them? With physics, but we don't know about any upper limit to heat, because at a certain point, measurement becomes meaningless. Beyond that, they lost me with talk about how temperature may be a loop of some kind.    

Space Explainer takes us through temperature extremes on earth and elsewhere, narrated by cartoon paper doll scientists on cartoon popsicle sticks, for some reason. (via

Laughing Squid)

items.title: The Invisible Servants of The Elms
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
It's hard to believe, but this 60,000 square foot mansion is sometimes referred to as a summer cottage. This is

The Elms in Newport, Rhode Island, built as a summer getaway for Edward Julius Berwind. Sure, it's big, but to guests it was a lot smaller on the inside than the outside. They wouldn't even notice that, because of the sheer size and opulence of the home. The rest of the house was hidden, because that's where the huge staff lived and worked. The interior was designed so that you never saw the work going on; the cleaning, cooking, and serving just happened as if by magic.

While the servants' quarters and work spaces are plain compared to the family and guest spaces at The Elms, they still look quite fancy to the modern eye. Architectural Digest shows us many of the engineering tricks and illusions that kept the dirty work behind genteel living hidden in The Elms.

items.title: Being the Queen Can Be Miserable
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content: Disney movies make little girls want to grow up to be a princess. They have beautiful dresses, loyal servants, a magical fairy godmother, and they end up marrying the prince of her dreams. But then what? Eventually you'll be a queen, and the lives of real queens were anything but fun. In real life as a queen, you didn't get to choose who you marry, possibly a prince or king who may be quite inbred, and you might not even speak the same language. Then your duty was to bear children of royal blood. Plenty of people wanted to kill your spouse or children or even you, and the rest of them wanted something from you. Meanwhile, you had to keep up the decorum expected from royalty. Your subjects might not even like you. It was a lifelong sentence of no privacy or agency.

items.title: Herbie
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Herbie is a triangular cat. He came from an animal shelter with a rare condition that makes his ears stick out to the sides instead of standing up on his head, leaving him looking somewhat like Dobby the house elf. He can't move his ears. But even more concerning is that Herbie is unable to close his eyes! He doesn't blink, and he sleeps with his eyes open, although his third eyelid does give him some protection. 

Herbie was diagnosed with bilateral facial nerve paralysis. He also has mild cerebellar hypoplasia, so he needs a special human to look after him. His foster mother became an expert at caring for him and now he's a permanent member of the family. You can see more of Herbie at Instagram.

items.title: Nikon Small World in Motion Winning Video May Be AI
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Nikon announced the winners of their annual Small World in Motion competition last week. The winning video was from Dr. Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in Beijing. The video shows "abnormal beating of airway cilia from a child with Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD), a genetic disorder affecting respiratory function." The above video shows the top five videos from the competition.

However, as soon as the winner was announced, other scientists started crying foul. The cilia seem to be the wrong size, and some structures seem to disappear at times. One researcher ran the video through Google Gemini and found an invisible watermark that may indicate the video was generated by artificial intelligence. Dr. Xu responded to the criticism, but since then, his comments at LinkedIn and his entire profile have been deleted. Nikon says it is re-reviewing the video and supplemental information about it. Read about the kerfluffle in the Small World in Motion winner's seat at PetaPixel.  (via Damn Interesting)

items.title: The World's Biggest Manmade Hole
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
The Bingham Canyon Mine in Utah is the biggest hole that humans have ever dug. Copper was discovered in the area in 1848, and they've been digging it out ever since. An open-pit mine proved to be the easiest way to extract the massive seam of low-grade porphyry copper ore, which also yields some gold, silver, lead, molybdenum, platinum, and palladium. The key to reaching it was explosives. What could possibly go wrong? 

Let's count: the danger of the explosives, the sheer work put into the project, the extra work to extract copper and other metals from the 400,000 tons of material removed every day, toxic chemicals exposed (it's a Superfund site), displaced residents, contaminated groundwater, the threat of flooding, and the danger of collapse. There's probably more, but the mine is quite profitable, even after all this time, so they'll keep digging the world's biggest hole even bigger. The video is only 5:37; the rest is an ad.
